# Kāḷabāhujātaka (Ja 329)

**ID:** Ja 329
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Kāḷabāhujātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Monkey Black-Arm
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja329
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kāḷabāhujātaka* (Ja 329) is a narrative included in the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon [SuttaCentral]. The story was delivered by the Buddha while residing at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana) in Rājagaha concerning Devadatta's loss of gain and honour after his failed hostility against the Buddha, including the inciting of archers and the release of the elephant Nālāgiri [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. 

In the tale of the past, the Bodhisatta was born as a wise parrot named Rādha living in the palace of the king of Benares alongside his younger brother Poṭṭhapāda [Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897; Vassiliades 2016]. When a forester presents the king with a large black monkey named Kālabāhu, the monkey receives lavished gifts and attention, eclipsing the parrots [Cowell 1897]. While Poṭṭhapāda becomes distressed and proposes fleeing to the forest, the Bodhisatta counsels patience, reflecting on the impermanence of worldly conditions (*aṭṭha lokadhammā*, such as fame and disrepute) and foretelling that the monkey's erratic antics will soon frighten the royal children [Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897]. When Kālabāhu subsequently terrifies the young princes with grimaces and ear-shaking, the king orders him driven out, restoring the parrots to their former honour [Cowell 1897]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), Kālabāhu is identified as Devadatta, Poṭṭhapāda as Ānanda, and Rādha as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1883].

Textual reuse analyses by DharmaNexus demonstrate significant overlap between the verses and commentary in the third volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* and cross-corpus links sharing passages with the *Aṭṭhakanipāta* of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 8) [DharmaNexus]. In later canonical commentary, the text is cited in the *Attadaṇḍasuttaniddesa* (Mnd 15) [SuttaCentral].

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Tatiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a3) (§2.4–3.4 ↔ §764–767); Aṭṭhakanipāta (AN 8) (§2.1–2.3 ↔ §5.2.1–5.2.3)
